sources.title: Call of Duty publisher apologizes for using real footage of Itaewon crowd crush | Yonhap News Agency
sources.text:
Call of Duty publisher apologizes for using real footage of Itaewon crowd crush | Yonhap News Agency Go to Contents Go to Navigation Facebook X More Pinterest Linked in Tumblr Reddit Facebook Messenger Copy URL URL is copied. OK SEOUL, Oct. 30 (Yonhap) -- The makers behind the Call of Duty video game apologized Friday for using real footage of the deadly 2022 Seoul crowd crush in its latest installment of the game and agreed to remove the footage. A short clip showing a paramedic performing CPR on a crowd crush victim lying on the street appeared in the opening moments of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4. The footage was used to depict a scenario of civilian casualties during a fictional war with North Korea. "We deeply apologize to the victims and their bereaved families who must have suffered, as well as to everyone who we have caused concern," Activision Publishing Inc. said in a notice to local reporters. "The footage will be removed in our update set to be rolled out on Nov. 12." The publisher added it had no plans to evoke tragic events, including the Itaewon crowd crush, when using news footage in its games, nor had it intended to ignore the pain caused by the accident. A total of 159 people were killed in a narrow alleyway in Seoul's night life district of Itaewon during Halloween festivities on Oct. 29, 2022. Bereaved families of the victims have criticized the game publisher for "lacking common sense" by using such footage and demanded a complete removal of the clip. A screen capture from the Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 game, which featured real footage of the Itaewon crowd crush that claimed the lives of 159 people on Oct. 29, 2022. sources.title: (2nd LD) N. Korean hackers blamed for record US$6.36 bln Binance cryptocurrency theft: U.S. firm | Yonhap News Agency
sources.text:
(2nd LD) N. Korean hackers blamed for record US$6.36 bln Binance cryptocurrency theft: U.S. firm | Yonhap News Agency Go to Contents Go to Navigation Facebook X More Pinterest Linked in Tumblr Reddit Facebook Messenger Copy URL URL is copied. OK (ATTN: UPDATES with comments from Trump at bottom) By Chang Dong-woo WASHINGTON, Oct. 30 (Yonhap) -- North Korean hackers purportedly stole an estimated US$6.36 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, in what would be the biggest cryptocurrency theft on record, according to a U.S. blockchain intelligence firm. TRM Labs said Thursday's attack against Binance was most likely carried out by TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group, which stole digital assets from Binance across 10 blockchain networks. Most of the funds were taken in about 20 minutes, it said. The firm said it had "high confidence" that the group was behind the attack, citing its analysis of cryptocurrency transactions and similarities with previous North Korean hacking operations. According to TRM Labs, the hackers began preparing for the attack at least 36 hours in advance. The firm believes they gained access to systems used to authorize cryptocurrency transfers, allowing them to move funds without permission. This file photo from the Associated Press shows the corporate logo of Binance. (PHOTO NOT FOR SALE) (Yonhap) TRM Labs said about $2.7 billion in stolen assets had been frozen through cooperation among cryptocurrency companies and blockchain operators. However, the hackers still controlled roughly $2.4 billion worth of Bitcoin and Ethereum, two major cryptocurrencies. The firm warned that the hackers could try to hide the origins of the stolen funds by moving them between different blockchain networks and cryptocurrency trading platforms. The attack would far exceed the $1.5 billion stolen from cryptocurrency exchange Bybit in February 2025, which the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation attributed to TraderTraitor. U.S. officials have pointed out in the past that North Korea relies on networks of its nationals abroad and foreign-based facilitators, including in China, Russia, Cambodia and Vietnam, to launder stolen digital assets into fiat currency for procurement activities and for funding its weapons of mass destruction programs. Richard Teng, co-CEO of Binance, wrote on X that the company was "working non-stop" to resolve the issue. "We are committed to covering all hacked losses through our company funds. Your assets are safe," he wrote. Teng added that Binance has reserved over $6.34 billion of company funds to cover the stolen assets. Of those funds, $5 billion was already held in the exact token assets that were impacted, he said. According to Bloomberg News, the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation said it is aware of the incident and is coordinating with its partners "to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts and coordinate appropriate investigative steps." U.S. President Donald Trump also acknowledged that the case was being pursued by law enforcement authorities. "We don't know. We are looking at that, the hack with Binance," Trump said when asked whether North Korean hackers could be the perpetrators. This graphic image illustrates a North Korea-backed cyberattack threat.
